claim: Proteins can self-organize into spatial patterns via non-linear dynamic interactions on cellular membranes.
source: Proteins can self-organize into spatial patterns via non-linear dynamic interactions on cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the context for the study.

claim: Modelling and simulations have shown that small GTPases can generate patterns by coupling guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF) to effectors, generating a positive feedback of GTPase activation and membrane recruitment.
source: Modelling and simulations have shown that small GTPases can generate patterns by coupling guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF) to effectors, generating a positive feedback of GTPase activation and membrane recruitment.
evidence: This claim references prior computational work on GTPase patterning mechanisms.

claim: A minimal system consisting of Rab5, RabGDI and a complex of full length Rabex5/Rabaptin5 was necessary to pattern Rab5 into membrane domains.
source: A minimal system consisting of Rab5, RabGDI and a complex of full length Rabex5/Rabaptin5 was necessary to pattern Rab5 into membrane domains.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Rab5 patterning required a lipid membrane composition mimicking that of early endosomes.
source: Rab5 patterning required a lipid membrane composition mimicking that of early endosomes, with PI(3)P enhancing membrane recruitment of Rab5 and acyl chain packing being critical for domain formation.
evidence: This finding is supported by experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6 comparing different lipid compositions.

claim: PI(3)P enhances membrane recruitment of Rab5.
source: Rab5 patterning required a lipid membrane composition mimicking that of early endosomes, with PI(3)P enhancing membrane recruitment of Rab5 and acyl chain packing being critical for domain formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing increased Rab5 recruitment to membranes containing PI(3)P.

claim: Acyl chain packing is critical for Rab5 domain formation.
source: Rab5 patterning required a lipid membrane composition mimicking that of early endosomes, with PI(3)P enhancing membrane recruitment of Rab5 and acyl chain packing being critical for domain formation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in Figure 6 and Table 5 showing that sphingomyelin and cholesterol are necessary for domain formation.

claim: The prevalence of GEF/effector coupling in nature suggests a possible universal system for small GTPase patterning involving both protein and lipid interactions.
source: The prevalence of GEF/effector coupling in nature suggests a possible universal system for small GTPase patterning involving both protein and lipid interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and broader biological context.

claim: Symmetry breaking of the plasma membrane in Caenorhabditis elegans is caused by PAR proteins that sort into distinct anterior and posterior cortical domains.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, symmetry breaking of the plasma membrane is caused by PAR proteins that sort into distinct anterior and posterior cortical domains and generate cell polarity (Kemphues et al., 1988; Motegi and Seydoux, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In xylem cells, ROP11 is organized into multiple domains on the PM where it interacts with cortical microtubules to regulate cell wall architecture.
source: In xylem cells, ROP11 is organized into multiple domains on the PM where it interacts with cortical microtubules to regulate cell wall architecture (Yang and Lavagi, 2012; Oda and Fukuda, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: On early endosomes, Rab5 exists in domains where it regulates vesicle tethering and fusion.
source: On early endosomes (EE), Rab5 exists in domains where it regulates vesicle tethering and fusion (McBride et al., 1999; Sönnichsen et al., 2000; Franke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Small GTPases use GTP/GDP binding to act as an ON/OFF switch.
source: Small GTPases use GTP/GDP binding to act as an ON/OFF switch.
evidence: This is established knowledge about small GTPase function.

claim: The cycling between GTP and GDP-bound states is regulated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase activating proteins (GAPs).
source: The cycling between GTP and GDP-bound states is regulated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) (Bos et al., 2007; Cherfils and Zeghouf, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most small GTPases are post-translationally modified by lipid chains which allow them to associate with membranes.
source: Most small GTPases are post-translationally modified by lipid chains which allow them to associate with membranes (Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The inactive GTPase forms a high-affinity complex with guanine dissociation inhibitor (GDI), regulating membrane cycling.
source: The inactive GTPase forms a high-affinity complex with guanine dissociation inhibitor (GDI), regulating membrane cycling (Sasaki et al., 1990; Ghomashchi et al., 1995; Cherfils and Zeghouf, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nucleotide exchange to GTP or a GTP analogue prevents interaction with GDI and frees the GTPase to interact with the membrane.
source: Nucleotide exchange to GTP or a GTP analogue prevents interaction with GDI and frees the GTPase to interact with the membrane, where it can recruit effector proteins and mediate downstream activities (Wu et al., 2010; Langemeyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon hydrolysis of GTP to GDP the GTPase is once again available for extraction from the membrane by GDI.
source: Upon hydrolysis of GTP to GDP the GTPase is once again available for extraction from the membrane by GDI (Rak et al., 2004; Ghomashchi et al., 1995; Pylypenko et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Small GTPase patterning can arise from the coupling of GEF activity and effector binding.
source: It has been proposed that small GTPase patterning can arise from the coupling of GEF activity and effector binding (Horiuchi et al., 1997; Zerial and McBride, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An active GTPase can recruit its own GEF, creating a local, positive feedback loop of GTPase activation and membrane recruitment.
source: In this way, an active GTPase can recruit its own GEF, creating a local, positive feedback loop of GTPase activation and membrane recruitment.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the GEF/effector coupling model.

claim: Self-organizing systems that form spatial patterns on membranes often exhibit non-linear dynamics of membrane recruitment and activation.
source: In general, self-organizing systems that form spatial patterns on membranes often exhibit such non-linear dynamics of membrane recruitment and activation (Halatek et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Rab5 GEF, Rabex5 is found in complex with the Rab5 effector Rabaptin5.
source: The Rab5 GEF, Rabex5 is found in complex with the Rab5 effector Rabaptin5. (Horiuchi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Cdc42 GEF Cdc24 is coupled to the effector Bem1.
source: Similarly, the Cdc42 GEF Cdc24 is coupled to the effector Bem1 (Chenevert et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Computational modelling revealed a Turing-type mechanism of pattern formation by a minimal system composed of Cdc42, the Bem1/Cdc24 complex and GDI.
source: Computational modelling revealed a Turing-type mechanism of pattern formation by a minimal system composed of Cdc42, the Bem1/Cdc24 complex and GDI (Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008; Goryachev and Leda, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior computational work.

claim: The ROP11 GEF, ROPGEF4, forms a dimer that catalyzes nucleotide exchange but also interacts with the active ROP11.
source: In plants, the ROP11 GEF, ROPGEF4, forms a dimer that catalyzes nucleotide exchange but also interacts with the active ROP11 (Nagashima et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rabex5 is a 57 kDa Vps9 domain containing GEF for Rab5.
source: Rabex5 is a 57 kDa Vps9 domain containing GEF for Rab5 (Horiuchi et al., 1997; Delprato and Lambright, 2007; Lauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rabaptin5 is a 99 kDa protein with multiple protein-protein interaction sites that colocalizes with Rab5 on EE and is essential for endosome fusion.
source: Rabaptin5 is a 99 kDa protein with multiple protein-protein interaction sites that colocalizes with Rab5 on EE and is essential for endosome fusion (Stenmark et al., 1995; Horiuchi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: As Rabaptin5 forms a dimer in solution, the complex is a tetramer of two Rabaptin5 and two Rabex5 subunits.
source: As Rabaptin5 forms a dimer in solution, the complex is a tetramer of two Rabaptin5 and two Rabex5 subunits (Lauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction with Rabaptin5 has been shown to increase Rabex5 GEF activity and produce structural rearrangements in Rabex5.
source: The interaction with Rabaptin5 has been shown to increase Rabex5 GEF activity and produce structural rearrangements in Rabex5 (Delprato et al., 2004; Delprato and Lambright, 2007; Lippé et al., 2001; Horiuchi et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 2014; Lauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: By binding active Rab5, Rabaptin5 localizes the enhanced GEF activity of Rabex5 in the vicinity of active Rab5, thereby creating the positive feedback loop.
source: By binding active Rab5, Rabaptin5 localizes the enhanced GEF activity of Rabex5 in the vicinity of active Rab5, thereby creating the positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on known protein interactions.

claim: Rabex5 can be recruited to EE via binding to Ubiquitin via two distinct Ubiquitin binding domains near the N-terminus.
source: In addition, Rabex5 can be recruited to EE via binding to Ubiquitin via two distinct Ubiquitin binding domains near the N-terminus (Penengo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ubiquitin binding enhances GEF activity toward Rab5 helping to initiate the positive feedback loop on endosomes carrying ubiquitinated cargo.
source: Interestingly, Ubiquitin binding enhances GEF activity toward Rab5 helping to initiate the positive feedback loop on endosomes carrying ubiquitinated cargo (Lauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Artificially targeting Rabex5 to mitochondria resulted in Rab5 recruitment to these organelles.
source: Blümer et al., 2013 observed that artificially targeting Rabex5 to mitochondria resulted in Rab5 recruitment to these organelles, suggesting that Rabex5 can be sufficient for localizing Rab5 to a membrane compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rab5 associates with the membrane by two 20-carbon geranylgeranyl chains attached at the C-terminus of the protein.
source: Rab5 associates with the membrane by two 20-carbon geranylgeranyl chains attached at the C-terminus of the protein (Farnsworth et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that both cholesterol and PI(3)P accumulate in the vicinity of Rab5.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that both cholesterol and PI(3)P accumulate in the vicinity of Rab5, and predicted a direct interaction with PI(3)P mediated by an Arg located in the flexible hypervariable region (HVR) between the C-terminal lipidation and the conserved GTPase domain (Edler et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: A direct interaction between Rab5 and PI(3)P is mediated by an Arg located in the flexible hypervariable region.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that both cholesterol and PI(3)P accumulate in the vicinity of Rab5, and predicted a direct interaction with PI(3)P mediated by an Arg located in the flexible hypervariable region (HVR) between the C-terminal lipidation and the conserved GTPase domain (Edler et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: Upon GDP/GTP exchange, Rab5 is directly transferred from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5.
source: Upon GDP/GTP exchange Rab5 is directly transferred from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5 - a mechanistic basis for positive feedback of Rab5 activation
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by HDX-MS experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nucleotide exchange causes dramatic stabilization of Val24-Leu38, Leu130-Leu137 and Met160-Met168 in Rab5, encompassing the P-loop and parts of β5, α4 and β6.
source: Focusing first on Rab5, we could see evidence of nucleotide exchange from the dramatic stabilization of Val24-Leu38, Leu130-Leu137 and Met160-Met168, encompassing the P-loop and parts of β 5, α4 and β 6 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A: dark blue), which, together, make up most of the direct interaction sites with GTP.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nucleotide exchange causes stabilization of Gln60-Phe71 in Rab5, parts of β2 and β3, consistent with the binding of Rabaptin5.
source: In addition, we saw stabilization of Gln60-Phe71, parts of β 2 and β 3 (sky blue and pale green), consistent with the binding of Rabaptin5 (Zhu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Indication of binding to Rabaptin5 was observed after only 1 min of reaction, providing evidence of a direct hand-off of active Rab5 from the Rabex5 catalytic domain to Rabaptin5.
source: Indication of binding to Rabaptin5 was observed after only 1 min of reaction, thus providing evidence of a direct hand-off of active Rab5 from the Rabex5 catalytic domain to Rabaptin5 (See Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nucleotide exchange causes destabilization of Ile177-Asp200, α5 in Rab5, suggesting a structural rearrangement of the C-terminal HVR.
source: Interestingly, we also saw a destabilization of Ile177-Asp200, α5 (yellow), suggesting a structural rearrangement of the C-terminal HVR.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stabilization was observed in both regions of Rabaptin5 known to bind Rab5, providing further evidence of Rab5 binding to Rabaptin5 after the nucleotide exchange reaction.
source: We saw stabilization in both of the regions known to bind Rab5, thus providing further evidence of Rab5 binding to Rabaptin5 after the nucleotide exchange reaction.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: EE-MCBs incubated with 10 nM GFP-Rab5/GDI showed membrane recruitment of GFP-Rab5 with a random distribution.
source: EE-MCBs incubated with 10 nM GFP-Rab5/GDI showed membrane recruitment of GFP-Rab5 with a random distribution (see Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The addition of GDI and Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP in the presence GDP removed GFP-Rab5 from the membrane.
source: The addition of GDI and Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP in the presence GDP removed GFP-Rab5 from the membrane (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The addition of GDI and Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP in the presence of GTP produced a redistribution of GFP-Rab5 on the membrane into discrete clusters or domains.
source: However, the same reaction in the presence of GTP produced a striking redistribution of GFP-Rab5 on the membrane into discrete clusters or domains (see Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The formation of GFP-Rab5 domains required GDI in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the formation of GFP-Rab5 domains required GDI in a concentration-dependent manner (see Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Domains with a mean diameter of 1.32 µm were detected on MCBs incubated with GFP-Rab5/GDI, GDI, Rabex5/Rabaptin5, and GTP but not GDP.
source: Domains with a mean diameter of 1.32 µm were detected on MCBs incubated with GFP-Rab5/GDI, GDI, Rabex5/Rabaptin5, and GTP but not GDP.
evidence: This is quantified in Table 2 based on image analysis of data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rab5 domains formed with a characteristic density of ~4.7 domains/EE-MCB.
source: They formed with a characteristic density of ~4.7 domains/EE-MCB and were rarely found adjacent to one another.
evidence: This is quantified in Table 2 based on image analysis of data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a marked increase in GFP-Rab5 signal within the segmented domain as compared to the area outside.
source: A critical hallmark of the reconstituted domains is a marked increase in GFP-Rab5 signal within the segmented domain as compared to the area outside (See Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Domains appear to be nucleated within the first minute of the reaction and then grow linearly in intensity until ~5 min after initiation of the reaction.
source: Domains appear to be nucleated within the first minute of the reaction (which we could not capture due to the imaging setup) and then grow linearly in intensity until ~5 min after initiation of the reaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: After ~5 min, individual domains increase in GFP-Rab5 signal intensity slowly or not at all, suggesting that some domains reach saturation.
source: After this point individual domains increase in GFP-Rab5 signal intensity slowly or not at all, suggesting that some domains reach saturation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse data shown in Figure 2H and involves inference about saturation.

claim: When whole MCBs were bleached, domains recovered in the same locations after photobleaching indicating that there is a constant exchange of GFP-Rab5 with solution.
source: Interestingly, when whole MCBs were bleached domains recovered in the same locations after photobleaching indicating that there is a constant exchange of GFP-Rab5 with solution (See Figure 2I, Figure 2—Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Rab5 domain formation requires Rabex5/Rabaptin5 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: We observed that, similar to GDI, Rab5 domain formation requires Rabex5/Rabaptin5 in a concentration-dependent manner (see Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E and Table 3, which summarizes the conditions shown in Figure 3A,B & C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A-E and quantified in Table 3.

claim: The Rabex5/Rabaptin5 complex localizes to the Rab5 domain.
source: Next, we verified that the Rabex5/Rabaptin5 complex indeed localizes to the Rab5 domain. For this, we used a fluorescent Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP complex and observed both enrichment of Rabaptin5-RFP signal inside the domain (See Figure 4A) and colocalization with GFP-Rab5 (See Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP showed some degree of membrane association in the absence of other factors, however this was significantly lower than the signal observed inside the GFP-Rab5 domains.
source: Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP also showed some degree of membrane association in the absence of other factors (See Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), however this was significantly lower than the signal observed inside the GFP-Rab5 domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Neither full-length Rabex5 nor the Rabex5 catalytic domain alone were sufficient to form domains in the presence of Rab5, GDI and GTP.
source: In the presence of Rab5, GDI and GTP, neither full-length Rabex5 nor the Rabex5 catalytic domain (Rabex5CAT) alone were sufficient to form domains (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Rabaptin5 alone was not capable of forming domains.
source: Similarly, Rabaptin5 alone was not capable of forming domains (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Rabex5CAT plus full-length Rabaptin5 did not support Rab5 domain formation.
source: Unlike the full length Rabex5/Rabaptin5 complex, Rabex5CAT plus full-length Rabaptin5 did not support Rab5 domain formation (compare Figure 3J and I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3I and 3J.

claim: Direct coupling of GEF activity and effector binding is essential for Rab5 domain formation.
source: This suggests that direct coupling of GEF activity and effector binding is essential for Rab5 domain formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing that separated components cannot form domains.

claim: Neither the domain diameter nor the area differed significantly when decreasing Rabex5/Rabaptin5 concentration, but the mean intensity of domains decreased with decreasing concentration of Rabex5/Rabaptin5.
source: Interestingly, neither the domain diameter nor the area differed significantly when decreasing Rabex5/Rabaptin5 concentration, but the mean intensity of domains decreased with decreasing concentration of Rabex5/Rabaptin5 (See Figure 3E and Table 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3E and Table 3.

claim: The presence of PI(3)P enhances Rab5 recruitment, either by facilitating the dissociation of Rab5 from GDI or by inhibiting the extraction of Rab5 by GDI.
source: This suggests that the presence of PI(3)P enhances Rab5 recruitment, either by facilitating the dissociation of Rab5 from GDI or by inhibiting the extraction of Rab5 by GDI.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments shown in Figure 5 comparing membranes with and without PI(3)P.

claim: The presence of cholesterol appeared to improve Rab5 recruitment to the simple lipid composition, although to a lesser degree than PI(3)P.
source: The presence of cholesterol (CH) appeared to also improve Rab5 recruitment to the simple lipid composition, although to a lesser degree than PI(3)P (See Figure 5F; PC/PS/CH-MCB vs PC/PS-MCB, See Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Domain formation was most efficient on EE-MCBs with 1 mol% PI(3)P, less efficient on EE-MCBs with 0 mol% PI(3)P and completely abolished on PC/PS membranes regardless of PI(3)P content.
source: Strikingly, domain formation was most efficient on EE-MCBs with 1 mol% PI(3)P, less efficient on EE-MCBs with 0 mol% PI(3)P and completely abolished on PC/PS membranes regardless of PI(3)P content (see Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 4 which summarizes the conditions shown in Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 6 and quantified in Table 4.

claim: Domains formed on EE membranes in the absence of PI(3)P had a drastically reduced mean domain intensity (508.32 ± 143.37) compared to domains formed in the presence of PI(3)P (mean domain intensity 1269.32 ± 556.54).
source: Domains formed on EE membranes in the absence of PI(3)P had a drastically reduced mean domain intensity (508.32 ± 143.37) compared to domains formed in the presence of PI(3)P (mean domain intensity 1269.32 ± 556.54) (See Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The membrane association of Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP was not found to be similarly lipid composition-dependent.
source: Importantly, the membrane association of Rabex5/Rabaptin5-RFP was not found to be similarly lipid composition-dependent (See Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No domain formation could be observed for PC/PS-MCBs while both PC/PS/CH-MCBs and PC/PS/CH/PlasmPE-MCBs showed infrequent and only low-intensity domains compared to EE-MCBs.
source: Interestingly, no domain formation could be observed for PC/PS-MCBs while both PC/PS/CH-MCBs and PC/PS/CH/PlasmPE-MCBs showed infrequent and only low-intensity domains compared to EE-MCBs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and quantified in Table 5.

claim: Only PC/PS/CH/SM-MCBs were able to recapitulate domains with a GFP signal intensity similar to that observed on EE-MCBs, although the prevalence of domains on PC/PS/CH/SM-MCBs was still reduced.
source: Only PC/PS/CH/SM-MCBs were able to recapitulate domains with a GFP signal intensity similar to that observed on EE-MCBs, although the prevalence of domains on PC/PS/CH/SM-MCBs was still reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and quantified in Table 5.

claim: Staining EE-MCBs with C-laurdan in the absence of proteins and imaging by confocal microscopy did not reveal the presence of macroscopic pre-existing liquid ordered (LO) domains.
source: Staining EE-MCBs with C-laurdan in the absence of proteins and imaging by confocal microscopy, as described by Dodes Traian et al., 2012 did not reveal the presence of macroscopic pre-existing liquid ordered (LO) domains (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from an experiment.

claim: Membrane recruitment and extraction (via GDI) together with coupling of GEF and effector activities (via Rabex5/Rabaptin5) are sufficient to reconstitute domain organization of Rab5 in vitro.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that membrane recruitment and extraction (via GDI) together with coupling of GEF and effector activities (via Rabex5/Rabaptin5) are sufficient to reconstitute domain organization of Rab5 in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Geranylgeranylated Rab5 was observed to be recruited to EE-like membranes from the Rab5/GDI complex.
source: Geranylgeranylated Rab5 was observed to be recruited to EE-like membranes from the Rab5/GDI complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of other factors Rab5 was randomly distributed in the plane of the membrane, but upon the addition of GDI, Rabex5/Rabaptin5 and GTP, it reorganized into discrete domains in a GTP-dependent manner.
source: Whereas in the absence of other factors Rab5 was randomly distributed in the plane of the membrane, upon the addition of GDI, Rabex5/Rabaptin5 and GTP, it reorganized into discrete domains in a GTP-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Key to Rab5 domain formation was the 'handover' of Rab5 from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5 and the lipid composition of early endosomes.
source: Key to Rab5 domain formation was the 'handover' of Rab5 from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5 and the lipid composition of early endosomes, suggesting a hitherto unknown cooperativity between lipids and Rab-dependent membrane self-organization.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Neither GEF activity nor effector binding alone were capable of supporting domain formation unless physically coupled in a complex.
source: Neither GEF activity nor effector binding alone were capable of supporting domain formation unless physically coupled in a complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 3F-J.

claim: In the course of nucleotide exchange, newly activated Rab5 is released from Rabex5 and immediately binds Rabaptin5 suggesting there is a direct delivery or 'handover' of Rab5 from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5.
source: We found that, in the course of nucleotide exchange, newly activated Rab5 is released from Rabex5 and immediately binds Rabaptin5 suggesting there is a direct delivery or 'handover' of Rab5 from Rabex5 to Rabaptin5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: This 'handover' is likely facilitated by the dimerization of the Rabex5/Rabaptin5 complex and presents a structural mechanism by which a positive feedback loop of Rab5 activation could be generated.
source: This 'handover' is likely facilitated by the dimerization of the Rabex5/Rabaptin5 complex and presents a structural mechanism by which a positive feedback loop of Rab5 activation could be generated.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the HDX-MS data and known complex structure.

claim: Other Rab5 GEFs that localize and recruit Rab5 to different intracellular compartments (e.g. GAPVD1 or RIN1 on clathrin-coated vesicles and the plasma membrane) have as of yet not been found to be coupled to effector activity.
source: Other Rab5 GEFs that localize and recruit Rab5 to different intracellular compartments (e.g. GAPVD1 or RIN1 on clathrin-coated vesicles and the plasma membrane; Tall et al., 2001; Semerdjieva et al., 2008 have as of yet not been found to be coupled to effector activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In vivo Rabex5/Rabaptin5 can be targeted to the EE by interaction of Rabex5 with ubiquitinated receptors and the binding of Ubiquitin to Rabex5 enhances nucleotide exchange activity.
source: In vivo Rabex5/Rabaptin5 can be targeted to the EE by interaction of Rabex5 with ubiquitinated receptors and the binding of Ubiquitin to Rabex5 enhances nucleotide exchange activity (Lee et al., 2006; Mattera et al., 2006; Penengo et al., 2006; Lauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ubiquitinated cargo can act not only to recruit Rabex5/Rabaptin5 but also potentially contribute to Rab5 domain formation and/or localization on the EE.
source: This implies that ubiquitinated cargo can act not only to recruit Rabex5/Rabaptin5 but also potentially contribute to Rab5 domain formation and/or localization on the EE.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known effects of ubiquitin binding.

claim: The membrane diffusion of multiple small GTPases has been shown to be integral in their capacity to self-organize.
source: The membrane diffusion of multiple small GTPases has been shown to be integral in their capacity to self-organize (Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008; Bruurs et al., 2015 and Bruurs et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In molecular dynamics simulations, Edler et al., 2017a suggest a direct interaction between Rab5 and PI(3)P and also observed accumulation of cholesterol in the proximity of Rab5.
source: In molecular dynamics simulations, Edler et al., 2017a suggest a direct interaction between Rab5 and PI(3)P and also observed accumulation of cholesterol in the proximity of Rab5.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: On the EE, PI(3)P is mainly produced by the activity of the class II PI3K complex, Vps34/Vps15, which is regulated by a direct interaction between Rab5 and Vps15.
source: On the EE, PI(3)P is mainly produced by the activity of the class II PI3K complex, Vps34/Vps15, which is regulated by a direct interaction between Rab5 and Vps15 (Christoforidis et al., 1999a; Christoforidis et al., 1999b; Murray et al., 2002; Falasca and Maffucci, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rab5 directly modifies the local lipid environment to stabilize itself on the membrane, thus providing yet another level of positive feedback in vivo.
source: This suggests that Rab5 directly modifies the local lipid environment to stabilize itself on the membrane, thus providing yet another level of positive feedback in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known regulation of PI3K by Rab5.

claim: The observation that simple, highly diffusive, PC/PS membranes do not support domain formation suggests that the EE lipid composition facilitates lateral lipid packing and protein-lipid interactions that are necessary for domain formation.
